questions.enonce_markdown: Identify and state the concept depicted by the above diagram. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**The concept is the paradox of thrift (also called the paradox of saving).**

Statement: if households, as a group, try to save more at every level of income, the result is not a higher amount of saving. Equilibrium national income falls, and with it the amount actually saved (and invested) ends up unchanged or lower than before. What is sensible for one household (saving more) is self-defeating for all households together.

questions.enonce_markdown: Using the diagram, briefly explain the concept identified in (a) above. (5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Reading the diagram.** The vertical axis shows saving and investment, the horizontal axis shows national income. $S_0$ is the initial saving function (upward sloping, negative at very low income), $S_1$ is the new saving function lying above and to the left of $S_0$, and $I$ is the investment function, which slopes upward and cuts the vertical axis at point $a$.

**Explanation.**

1. **Initial equilibrium.** National income is in equilibrium where planned saving equals planned investment, $S_0 = I$. This is at national income $Y_2$, with saving and investment equal to $SI_1$.
2. **Increase in the desire to save.** Households decide to save more out of every income, so the saving function shifts upward, from $S_0$ to $S_1$ (the arrows).
3. **Disequilibrium.** At $Y_2$, planned saving is now greater than planned investment: leakages exceed injections, so total spending is lower than output. Firms find unsold stocks, cut production and lay off workers, so incomes fall (by a multiple of the initial fall in spending).
4. **Fall in income and in investment.** As income falls, saving falls along $S_1$, and because investment is partly induced it falls as well along $I$. The process stops when $S_1 = I$ again, at the lower income $Y_1$.
5. **Result.** National income falls from $Y_2$ to $Y_1$ and the amount saved and invested falls from $SI_1$ to $SI_2$. The attempt to save more has led to less saving: this is the paradox.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) State two assumptions of the concept identified in (a) above. (2 marks)

(ii) Besides saving, list the other two leakages in an economy. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Two assumptions of the paradox of thrift** (any two):

1. The economy is below full employment, with spare capacity and (roughly) constant prices, so that output and income adjust to changes in spending (a Keynesian situation).
2. Planned investment does not rise to absorb the extra saving (investment depends on the level of income and is not stimulated by the fall in the interest rate), so that saving and investment are brought into equality by a change in income rather than in the interest rate.

Other acceptable assumptions: all (or most) households try to save more at the same time, and the economy is simple (closed, with no government), so that saving is the only leakage.

**(ii) The other two leakages (withdrawals)** are:

1. **Taxation** (taxes on income and spending paid to the government), and
2. **Imports** (spending on foreign goods and services, which leaves the circular flow).

questions.enonce_markdown: How can you conclude from the diagram that investment is both autonomous and induced? (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The investment function in the diagram can be written $I = a + bY$ with $b > 0$.

- **Autonomous investment.** The line $I$ **cuts the vertical axis at the positive value $a$**. Even when national income is zero, firms still invest the amount $a$: this part of investment does not depend on the level of income (it is decided on the basis of expectations, technology, government projects and so on). It is therefore autonomous.
- **Induced investment.** The line $I$ **slopes upward** instead of being a horizontal line: investment rises as national income rises (it is higher at $Y_2$, equal to $SI_1$, than at $Y_1$, equal to $SI_2$). The part of investment that changes with income, $bY$, is induced investment.

Because the line starts above the origin and rises with income, investment has both an autonomous component ($a$) and an induced component ($bY$). A horizontal line would show autonomous investment only, and a line through the origin induced investment only.

questions.enonce_markdown: State any four factors that can increase household savings in Cameroon. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Any four of the following:

1. **A rise in household disposable income** (higher wages, bigger cocoa, coffee or cotton revenues, remittances): the richer the household, the larger the part of income left after consumption.
2. **Higher interest rates or better returns on savings** deposits and savings products, which reward households for postponing consumption.
3. **Development of savings institutions**: more banks, microfinance institutions, credit unions and mobile-money services in towns and villages, together with traditional tontines (njangi), make saving easier and safer.
4. **Confidence in the financial system and macroeconomic stability** (stable prices, no bank failures, secure property), so that households trust institutions with their money.
5. **Expectation of future needs or uncertainty** (old age, illness, school fees, a poor harvest) combined with weak social security, which leads households to build a reserve.
6. **Financial education and a culture of saving**, and tax incentives or government savings schemes.
